title: fix duplicate EasyEDA pad connectivity
description: Fixes the issue of duplicate EasyEDA pad connectivity by ensuring that multiple geometries with the same pad number are treated as a single logical pin, eliminating synthetic ports and ambiguous connections.
body: ## Problem The EasyEDA converter treated every physical `PAD` geometry as a separate logical pin, even when several geometries had the same EasyEDA pad number. That produced synthetic source ports and duplicate aliases which do not exist on the component. For `C132561`, the source footprint contains eleven physical pad geometries: - signal pads `1` through `5` - six shell geometries, all numbered `6` The old conversion incorrectly emitted logical `pin6` through `pin11`. Pins `7`–`11` all received the same `pin6_alt1` alias, so the generated component had ambiguous, invented ports. EasyEDA pad numbers map footprint geometry to schematic pins. Multiple geometries carrying the same pad number therefore belong to the same logical terminal; they are not additional source pins. See the [EasyEDA footprint documentation](https://docs.easyeda.com/en/PCBLib/PCBLib-Create/). ## Before and after snapshots | `C132561` | Before | After | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Physical pad geometries | 11 | 11 | | Logical source ports | 11 | 6 | | Shell geometries | `pin6`–`pin11` | six shapes on `pin6` | | Synthetic ports | `pin7`–`pin11` | none | ### Rendered regression snapshots The visual fixture below is `C51950748`, which has nine physical exposed-pad geometries sharing EasyEDA pad number 29. The **before** images were rendered from base commit `2ef5112`; the **after** images were rendered from this PR at `74e921d`. #### Schematic | Before — invented pins 33–40 | After — one logical `EPAD` pin 29 | | --- | --- | | | | Before the fix, the repeated pad number created synthetic schematic pins 33–40 with the duplicate `pin29_alt1` label. After the fix, the schematic exposes one logical `EPAD` terminal at pin 29. #### PCB | Before | After | | --- | --- | | | | The PCB geometry is intentionally unchanged: all nine center copper pads remain. The fix changes their logical mapping so every center shape belongs to `pin29`; it does not remove or merge physical copper. ### Before ```tsx const pinLabels = { pin6: ["EH1"], pin7: ["pin6_alt1"], pin8: ["pin6_alt1"], pin9: ["pin6_alt1"], pin10: ["pin6_alt1"], pin11: ["pin6_alt1"], } // Six shell geometries were incorrectly assigned different logical ports. ``` ### After ```tsx const pinLabels = { pin6: ["EH"], } // The same six physical geometries correctly share logical pin 6. ``` The repeated `` entries above are physical copper shapes, not duplicate source ports. ## Root cause `convertEasyEdaJsonToCircuitJson` passed one label set per physical pad into `normalizePinLabels`. The normalizer avoided duplicate canonical pin numbers by renumbering later occurrences, so repeated pad numbers became synthetic pins. ## Fix - group numbered EasyEDA pad geometries by their original pad number before normalization - normalize each logical pad-number group once - emit one `source_port` per logical pin - preserve every physical SMT/plated-hole geometry and map each one back to its shared logical pin - keep unnumbered pads independent - add regression coverage using a real component with a split exposed pad - snapshot both schematic and PCB rendering for the repeated-pad fixture - update the affected `C2838502`, `C2913206`, and `C51950748` generated snapshots ## Impact Generated imports no longer expose invented or ambiguous pins. Split exposed pads, shell tabs, and other multi-geometry terminals retain all footprint copper while matching the logical connectivity declared by the EasyEDA source. ## Validation - `bunx tsc --noEmit` - `bun run build` - `bun run format:check` - `git diff --check` - focused regression suite: 12 passed, 0 failed - live `C132561` conversion: one logical `pin6` across six shell geometries - visual regression: one schematic `EPAD` terminal while all nine PCB pad shapes remain - all GitHub CI checks passed Fixes #411. This is a fresh-`main` replacement for #413, which currently conflicts with `main`. It follows the same source-pad semantics while using an existing real component fixture for regression coverage.

title: Infer pin attributes for imported chips
description: Infers conservative pin attributes for imported chip power, ground, and no-connect pins, emitting the inferred attributes in generated tscircuit components while skipping ambiguous or unsupported aliases.
body:
## Summary

- infer conservative `pinAttributes` for imported chip power, ground, and no-connect pins
- emit the inferred attributes in generated tscircuit components
- skip ambiguous or unsupported aliases rather than guessing
- update converter snapshots and add unit plus circuit-JSON integration coverage

## Why

EasyEDA imports previously emitted pin labels without electrical pin metadata. As a result, tscircuit checks reported imported IC pins as underspecified even when their labels clearly identified supply, ground, or no-connect pins.

## Impact

Imported chips now mark recognized `VCC`, `VDD`, `VIN`, and `VDDA` pins as requiring power; `GND`, `VSS`, `PGND`, and `AGND` pins as requiring ground; and `NC` pins as do-not-connect. Numbered variants are supported, while ambiguous multi-label pins remain unchanged.

## Validation

- `bun run format:check`
- `bun run build`
- `bun test` — 178 passed, 0 failed; 59 snapshots; 795 expectations
- `git diff --check`

body:
## Summary

Fixes JLCPCB mechanical keyboard switch imports that are incorrectly generated as generic `<chip>` components with malformed schematic symbols.

## What changed

- Detects keyboard-switch metadata from `KEY-TH_` and `KEY-SMD_` package identifiers.
- Generates `PushButtonProps` and `<pushbutton>` for mechanical keyboard switches.
- Preserves the imported footprint, supplier part number, and CAD model.
- Updates the `C49234237` regression fixture and schematic snapshot.
- Adds classification coverage for keyboard-switch metadata.

## Reproduction

JLCPCB part `C49234237` (`CPG151101D06`, brown mechanical keyboard switch) previously generated:

```tsx
import type { ChipProps } from "@tscircuit/props"

<chip>
```

This produced an oversized, malformed schematic symbol.

The corrected output generates:

```tsx
import type { PushButtonProps } from "@tscircuit/props"

<pushbutton>
```

## Validation

- `bun format`
- Focused `C49234237` conversion test
- Pushbutton category tests
- Updated schematic SVG snapshot

This PR both reproduces and fixes the import-classification and schematic-symbol issue.

title: Repro: trailing-hash active-low pin labels lose polarity
description: Adds a regression test to reproduce the issue where active-low pin labels lose their polarity due to the removal of trailing hashes in the conversion process.
body:
## Motivation

The raw EasyEDA data for JLCPCB part C490691 (FT232RL) marks active-low pins with a trailing `#`, including `DTR#`, `RTS#`, `RI#`, and `RESET#`.

The converter currently removes the trailing `#` without preserving its meaning. Generated labels such as `DTR` and `RESET` therefore appear as normal positive-logic signals instead of active-low signals.

![C490691 schematic with stripped active-low labels](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GokulPandi-M/easyeda-converter/codex/repro-active-low-trailing-hash/tests/convert-to-ts/__snapshots__/C490691-active-low-labels-stripped.snap.svg)

## Reproduction

- Confirms the raw EasyEDA source contains `DTR#` and `RESET#`.
- Confirms the generated TSX incorrectly contains `DTR` and `RESET` instead of `N_DTR` and `N_RESET`.
- Adds a schematic snapshot showing that the affected signals are rendered without active-low overlines.

This PR only adds regression coverage and does not implement the fix.

title: Fix document-layer tracks converted to silkscreen
description: Fixes the conversion of EasyEDA document-layer tracks to ensure they are preserved as fabrication notes instead of being incorrectly converted to silkscreen.
body:
## Motivation

EasyEDA Document-layer tracks are currently converted to PCB silkscreen. This can incorrectly add reference-only markings to the manufactured silkscreen.

This change preserves those tracks as fabrication notes, keeping them visible in tscircuit without including them in the physical silkscreen.

## Summary

- restrict EasyEDA TRACK-to-silkscreen conversion to layers 3 and 4
- preserve layer-12 document tracks as fabrication-note paths
- update the regression assertion and PCB SVG snapshots

Fixes the behavior reproduced in #449. The converter previously treated every non-courtyard TRACK as silkscreen; C136720 now keeps its right-side bracket as a visible fabrication note instead.

Verified against the current EasyEDA payload for C136720: two TRACKs are on TopSilkLayer (3), and the right-side bracket is on Document (12).

title: Preserve all pins on multi-pin inductors
description: Fixes the issue where multi-pin inductors were incorrectly converted to two-terminal inductors, resulting in lost physical terminals in the schematic.
body:
## Motivation

bug repro in #461.

[JLCPCB/LCSC C3273487](https://www.lcsc.com/product-detail/C3273487.html) is a four-pin Bourns SRF1280-101M coupled inductor. It was converted to the two-terminal `<inductor>` primitive, leaving two physical terminals unavailable in the schematic.

## Fix

- Use `<inductor>` only for two-pin inductors.
- Fall back to `<chip>` for multi-pin inductors so every physical terminal remains connectable.
- Avoid embedding the custom EasyEDA symbol for this fallback because combining its ports with `chip.pinLabels` creates duplicate source ports.
- Preserve normal two-pin inductor conversion.

The corrected C3273487 output contains exactly four source ports, four schematic ports, and four PCB pads.

 Corrected schematic

description: Uses pcbStyle.viaHoleDiameter and pcbStyle.viaPadDiameter as autorouter via constraints when minVia props are not set, ensuring consistent via sizes for both authored and generated vias.

## Summary

- use `pcbStyle.viaHoleDiameter` and `pcbStyle.viaPadDiameter` as autorouter via constraints when `minVia*` props are not set

body:
Fills in the gaps recorded by the base PR, and re-renders **the same snapshots from the same cameras**. Where they showed bare copper pads they now show the part; that diff is the review. The ledger goes from 35 entries to 3.

Most of this is dispatch, not geometry. `lib/Footprinter3d.tsx` switches on footprinter's `fn` and simply had no arm for these names, while a suitable body sat in `lib/` unreferenced — `SOT-563.tsx` and `BGA.tsx` had never been reachable at all, SC-70-4 shares SC-70-6's body, SOP and SSOP are SOIC with a different lead span, SON/WSON/VSON are DFNs, MLP and QUAD are QFNs.

Parameterised rather than aliased wherever the outline genuinely differs, since an alias reports a body that is not there:

- `SOT-223` takes its dimensions, so SOT-89 can use it at a third of the volume
- `TO-220` takes `mouldedTab`, because TO-220F encapsulates the tab
- LGA/MLP/QUAD read `w`/`h`, **not** `grid`: for those `grid` is a pad COUNT per side (`lga14` is 4x3 pads), so reading it as millimetres gave a 4 x 3 body for a part that is 2.4 x 2.9. Only `vson` states its outline as a grid.

Four new bodies, for parts nothing in the repo resembled: `DPAK` (TO-252 and TO-263 — a moulded body on an exposed tab, placed over the TAB pad because the footprint is asymmetric), `ElectrolyticCapacitor` (radial can; diameter from `d` or from the name, height derived and deliberately generous), `Potentiometer`, and `SmdPushButton` (whose actuator height is a separate prop, because that is what a lid has to clear).

`TO-92` is fixed separately in its own commit: it was translated 10.5mm up with 15mm leads, so a 4.5mm part measured 19.5mm end to end and floated above the board in every render.

`tests/body-coverage/body-envelope.test.ts` is the assertion the pictures cannot make — the height above the board, per package, against the datasheet outline. It also records the two placements known to be wrong (`to220` at 32.5mm, `breakoutheaders`' headers hanging below the board) with the values they measure, so fixing either fails the test and prompts the note to be deleted.

Still open, with reasons in the ledger: `jst` (only the ZH series has a body), `m2host` (footprinter reports no dimensions at all for it), `usbcmidmount` (`USB-C.tsx` draws with `Ellipsoid` and with `rotation` props on primitives; `lib/vanilla` implements neither and ignores the second SILENTLY rather than rejecting it, so reusing it would render the wrong shape).

body:
`getJscadModelForFootprint` accepts every footprinter name, builds whatever `lib/Footprinter3d.tsx` has a `case` for, and returns **cleanly with `geometries: []`** for the rest. Nothing throws, so a missing body is invisible at the point of use.

It stops being invisible as soon as something *measures* the result: `core`'s `measureFootprinterBody` feeds `create-fdm-enclosure`, which cannot tell whether a screw boss runs through a part that has no height. It reports `component_bounds_unknown` rather than guessing — so the gap is safe, but the clearance check simply does not run. The names affected are not a random tail: the SOT and TO families, electrolytics, potentiometers, switches and connectors, which are the tall parts an enclosure exists to clear.

**This PR fixes none of them.** It makes them reviewable:

- `tests/body-coverage/footprint-probes.ts` — the ledger. `NO_BODY` (copper features, where empty is the right answer), `PROBE` (names footprinter will not parse without a pin count), `MISSING_BODIES` (35 gaps, with a reason each).

title: fix: tolerate floating-point residue at pad boundaries
description: Fixes false missing-pad connection by allowing sub-nanometer floating-point residue at pad boundaries in circuit018 geometry calculations.
body:
## Summary

- accept only sub-nanometer floating-point residue when a trace endpoint lands mathematically on a pad boundary
- apply the numerical tolerance consistently to supported SMT-pad and plated-hole boundary shapes
- keep real physical gaps outside the pad rejected
- cover the exact reduced dataset01 circuit018 geometry

## Root cause

Dataset01 `circuit018` computes the preloaded trace endpoint and rectangular pad boundary through separate decimal calculations. Their mathematically equal coordinates differ by about `6e-16 mm`, so a strict comparison reports a false missing-pad connection.

This fixes the shared containment predicate in `@tscircuit/checks`. It does **not** move or normalize the trace endpoint, alter evaluator geometry, or special-case circuit018.

## Before / after

The stack merged while the snapshot-body update was being prepared. The visuals below are pinned to [upstream snapshot commit `719e845`](https://github.com/tscircuit/checks/commit/719e8451111f6eeb011c80952964b48d14a9d375), which adds only the requested paired visual artifacts around the same merged circuit018 regression.

| Before: false disconnect | After: valid boundary contact |
| --- | --- |
| ![circuit018 before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tscircuit/checks/719e8451111f6eeb011c80952964b48d14a9d375/tests/lib/__snapshots__/circuit018-pad-boundary-before.snap.svg) | ![circuit018 after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tscircuit/checks/719e8451111f6eeb011c80952964b48d14a9d375/tests/lib/__snapshots__/circuit018-pad-boundary-after.snap.svg) |

The before snapshot renders the actual error reported by `main` for this fixture. The after snapshot preserves the same copper geometry with no DRC overlay.

## Fix

`isPointInPad` allows `1e-9 mm` of numerical residue at pad boundaries. The regression separately checks that a point `1e-6 mm` outside remains rejected. Rounded SMT-pad and circular plated-hole boundary cases are covered as well.

title: Serialize copper primitives in binary PCB documents
description: Serializes Altium Fill, Polygon, and Region records into native binary .PcbDoc sections, preserving outlines, holes, and other properties while rejecting unsupported configurations.
body:
## What changed

- serialize Altium `Fill`, `Polygon`, and shape-based `Region` records into native binary `.PcbDoc` sections
- preserve region outlines, inner holes, layers, nets, polygon ownership, locks, and keepout flags
- reject unsupported region kinds, fields, duplicate fields, malformed contours, and missing hole vertices instead of writing lossy output
- render a polygon as outline-only when a Region references it, preventing the editable definition and poured copper from being filled twice
- render active standalone polygons with the same copper opacity as Region fills, while keeping shelved polygons outline-only
- add one focused creation test per primitive family plus focused raw SVG snapshots

## Why

`circuit-json-to-altium` needs native copper-pour output. Its converter owns the Circuit JSON mapping, but the native OLE/CFB record encoding belongs in `altiumts` so Altium format knowledge remains centralized and reusable.

Altium stores an editable polygon definition separately from its poured Region. The SVG renderer now paints one logical copper fill regardless of whether the input represents it as a standalone active Polygon or a Polygon associated with a Region. This keeps source and round-trip board colors consistent without double-filling generated pours.

## Validation

- `bun run format:check`
- `bun run lint`
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run build`
- 7 affected SVG tests pass locally, including SimpleFOC Mini, SimpleFOC Shield V3, Novena, linked Regions, standalone active Polygons, and shelved Polygons

title: Fix empty PCB wide strings
description: Fixes serialization of empty WideStrings6 entries to prevent shifting of subsequent text in Altium PCB files.
body:
## Summary

- encode empty `WideStrings6` entries using Altium's native declared-length-without-payload representation
- add a focused serialize-and-reparse regression test with non-empty text after an empty entry

## Root cause

`toAltiumUtf16LeBytes("")` returns the two-byte UTF-16 terminator. Native Altium files declare that length as `2` but omit the terminator payload. The serializer wrote both the declared length and those two bytes, while the parser correctly followed the native format and consumed no payload for lengths up to two. Every later entry was therefore shifted by two bytes.

This surfaced while converting several real open-source boards containing empty overlay text records and reparsing the generated `.PcbDoc` files.

## Validation

- `bun test tests/binary-pcb-empty-wide-string.test.ts tests/binary-pcb-document-creation.test.ts tests/binary-pcb-doc.test.ts`
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run lint`
- `bun run build`
- five real-board `circuit-json-to-altium` native round trips using this commit

The full local `bun test` run passed all 104 tests whose pinned references were available. The remaining 61 tests could not start because TI's `sprcal9` download returned HTTP 403, leaving that board and its 57 schematic sheets unavailable locally.

title: Serialize native-length via records
description: Serializes PCB vias to ensure they retain the native Altium 209-byte payload length, fixing issues with independent Altium tooling rejecting shortened records.
body:
## Summary

- serialize PCB via records with Altium's native 209-byte minimum payload
- retain the reserved via metadata tail even when optional stack fields are unset
- add a focused binary-layout regression test

## Root cause

The serializer emitted only the 31 bytes containing the currently modeled via fields. `altiumts` could parse those shortened records itself, but independent Altium tooling rejected the `Vias6/Data` entries because native Altium via payloads include a reserved metadata tail and are at least 209 bytes long.

This was found while round-tripping five open-source GitHub Altium boards through `circuit-json-to-altium` and parsing the generated documents with an independent implementation. Pads and tracks survived, but every generated via disappeared.

## Impact

Generated `.PcbDoc` files now retain vias when decoded by independent Altium parsers and more closely match the native record layout found in real Altium-authored boards.

## Validation

- `bun test tests/binary-pcb-via-native-layout.test.ts tests/binary-pcb-document-creation.test.ts`
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run format:check`
- independent `altium-toolkit` round-trip against the Novena eDP Adapter fixture: 214 source vias and 214 generated vias

description: Convert Circuit JSON rectangular, polygonal, and BRep copper pours into native Altium polygon and filled-region records, preserving pour nets, layers, holes, and openings, while ensuring consistent rendering and serialization.
body:
## Summary

- convert Circuit JSON rectangular, polygonal, and BRep copper pours into native Altium polygon and filled-region records
- preserve pour nets, outer/inner copper layers, BRep holes and curved edges, and explicit solder-mask openings
- include copper pours in the five pinned open-source board round trips and add a focused raw side-by-side SVG snapshot

## Why

Copper pours were previously omitted from generated Altium documents. This made converted boards look sparse and, more importantly, removed electrically significant copper. The converter now emits both an editable Altium polygon definition and its associated filled region.

The implementation follows the converter pipeline used elsewhere in the repository: parsing and normalization stay in a focused conversion module, while Altium binary-format serialization and rendering stay in `altiumts`.

title: Add connectsFromAbove / connectsFromBelow to pinHeaderProps
description: Adds aliases connectsFromAbove and connectsFromBelow to pinHeaderProps for clearer intent regarding the mounting side of pin headers, resolving to the layer property during parsing.
body:
Which side of the board a part is on is `layer`, and only `layer` — the 3D
model is always authored top-side and consumers flip it for a bottom-layer
component (3d-viewer repositions to -(z + pcbThickness) and rotates 180
degrees about X). But on a connector, "which side is this connected to from"
is the question actually being asked, and `layer: "bottom"` states the answer
in terms of the geometry rather than the intent.

These are aliases: `connectsFromAbove` is `layer: "top"`, `connectsFromBelow`
is `layer: "bottom"`. An explicit `layer` wins, and setting both is an error
rather than a silent precedence rule.

Resolved in the schema rather than by each consumer. core reads `layer` in
more than fifty places; an alias that only some of them understand is worse
than no alias, and after parsing there is one field to reason about again.

Worth stating what they are NOT: `invert` on a footprint string installs a
header BACKWARDS on whichever side it is on — long pins through the board
instead of short ones. That is a different axis, and conflating the two is
what produced tscircuit/jscad-electronics#333, where every through-hole pin
header rendered hanging beneath the board.

title: Say what `invert` and `faceup` mean, and deprecate `faceup`
description: Clarifies the meaning of invert and deprecates faceup, correcting misconceptions about their functionality in 3D model hints for footprints.
body:
Both are 3D-model hints on every footprint, and neither said enough to be
used correctly. Nothing in the ecosystem sets either one — the only
references anywhere are this schema and jscad-electronics' own examples —
so the descriptions were the whole specification, and they were wrong about
the one thing that matters.

`invert` said "hint to invert the orientation of the 3D model", which reads
as "flip it over" and so as a way to mount a part on the underside of the
board. It is not: which side a part is on is the component's `layer`, and
consumers implement that themselves (3d-viewer moves a bottom-layer part to
-(z + pcbThickness) and rotates it 180 degrees about X). A model that also
flipped itself would be flipped twice. What `invert` actually selects, and
what it selected when it was added, is which END of the pins passes through
the board: installed backwards, a header puts its LONG pins through.

`faceup` is deprecated. It was added a day after `invert`, sharing its
expression, and its only distinct effect was deleting the pins below the
board. On a through-hole footprint — which is plated HOLES — that produces a
part that cannot be soldered into its own land pattern, and the orientation
it described ("should face upwards, out of the top layer") is what a
correctly mounted header does by default.

Descriptions only; no behaviour changes here. jscad-electronics has been
made to match in tscircuit/jscad-electronics#333.

title: Fix dropped EasyEDA silkscreen rectangles in generated TSX
description: Fixes a data-preservation bug in EasyEDA footprint conversion where PCB silkscreen rectangles were parsed into Circuit JSON but dropped when generating the final TypeScript component.
body:
Fixes a data-preservation bug in EasyEDA footprint conversion: PCB silkscreen rectangles were parsed into Circuit JSON but dropped when generating the final TypeScript component.

## Impact

Generated footprints could silently lose package outlines and other rectangular silkscreen markings. The source data and intermediate soup retained these elements, but the TSX output omitted them, producing incomplete PCB footprints for affected EasyEDA components.

## Root cause

`generateFootprintTsx` emitted PCB holes, pads, vias, silkscreen paths, silkscreen text, fabrication paths, and courtyard outlines, but never emitted `pcb_silkscreen_rect` elements.

The regression is visible in the existing issue-#464 payload-variant fixture, which intentionally injects a small offset `RECT` shape. As noted in review, that offset comes from the fixture added in [#465](https://github.com/tscircuit/easyeda-converter/pull/465); it is source test data, not a new geometry transformation.

## Fix

- Emit each parsed `pcb_silkscreen_rect` as `<silkscreenrect>` in generated TSX.
- Preserve center position, width, height, stroke width, fill/stroke flags, and rotation.
- Update affected generated-TSX and PCB SVG expectations.
- Refresh the unrelated renderer-dependent 3D baselines that failed in CI.

## Regression coverage

- Package RECT parsing asserts the resulting `pcb_silkscreen_rect` data.
- Package RECT PCB rendering has a dedicated SVG snapshot.
- Existing conversion fixtures for C131337, C3178291, and C2943786 now assert the generated `<silkscreenrect>`.
- The issue-#464 payload-variant fixture continues to exercise the manually injected RECT path.

Validated with:

- `bun test tests/convert-package-rect.test.ts`
- `bun test tests/convert-to-ts/additional-payload-variants.test.ts`
- `bun test tests/convert-to-ts/C131337-to-ts.test.ts`

title: fix: preserve active-low pin names with N_ prefix instead of stripping #
description: Fixes the issue where active-low pin names with a trailing  were stripped, resulting in loss of signal semantics; now converts names like RESET to N_RESET, preserving their meaning in generated components and schematics.
body:
## Problem

EasyEDA uses a trailing `#` to mark active-low pins, for example `RESET#`, `DTR#`, `RTS#`, `E#`, and `SD#`. The converter previously removed that marker and emitted positive-logic names such as `RESET` and `DTR`, losing the signal semantics in generated tscircuit components and schematics.

## Fix

- Normalize leading or trailing active-low markers through one shared helper.
- Convert names such as `RESET#` to `N_RESET`, which tscircuit renders as an overlined active-low label.
- Avoid double-prefixing an already normalized name such as `N_ENABLE#`.
- Preserve a lone `#` instead of producing the invalid label `N_`.
- Update affected component outputs and schematic snapshots.
- Convert the merged C490691 reproduction into a regression test that verifies `N_DTR` and `N_RESET` end to end.

This changes pin-name semantics only; it does not alter pin coordinates, rotation, footprint geometry, or schematic layout calculations.

title: Fix custom-symbol port directions and trace endpoints
description: Fixes incorrect port directions and reconnects trace endpoints for custom symbols in React and Circuit JSON, ensuring accurate schematic representation and trace routing.
body:
## Summary

- honor explicit `direction` values on ports inside React and Circuit JSON custom symbols
- derive `side_of_component` from the same explicit direction instead of fallback schematic-box metadata
- reconnect solver-generated traces to the authoritative custom-symbol port center when the port lies on or outside the symbol boundary
- preserve intentional interior custom-symbol ports, which should remain projected to the symbol edge
- cover the behavior with the exact imported `DMT6007LFG_7` reproduction and schematic snapshots

## Root cause

### Port direction

A chip can retain fallback schematic-box placement metadata while rendering a custom symbol. Port rendering previously allowed that fallback side to override the custom symbol port's explicit `direction`. The emitted `schematic_port` could therefore face the wrong way, causing net labels such as `GATE` to be placed inward.

### Disconnected trace endpoint

The schematic solver can project a custom-symbol boundary port onto its routing-box edge. Core already reconnects solver-adjusted endpoints to authoritative `schematic_port` centers for text-expanded components, but custom symbols without text-expanded bounds were excluded. This left a visible gap between the `SOURCE` trace and the imported MOSFET's S3 port.

The endpoint reconciliation now also recognizes genuine React and Circuit JSON custom symbols. It remains restricted to ports on or outside the normal symbol boundary, so it does not draw traces through symbols that intentionally declare interior ports.

## Validation

- exact imported `DMT6007LFG_7` regression with and without traces/net labels
- custom-symbol interior-port regression
- ordinary RP2040, ATmega, schematic-section, and cross-sheet snapshot regressions
- `bunx tsc --noEmit`
- all 10 CI test shards, format check, type check, and smoke test pass

title: Fix internally connected custom-symbol ports
description: Fixes the inability to resolve internally connected pin groups from all ports owned by a component, including those nested inside a custom React symbol.
body:
## What changed

- Resolve internally connected pin groups from all ports owned by a component, including ports nested inside a custom React symbol.
- Preserve alias-based pin resolution and the existing missing-port error.
- Convert both exact DMT6007LFG-7 repros from expected failures into passing regression tests.

## Root cause

NormalComponent._getInternallyConnectedPins used portMap, which only searches direct child ports. Imported custom symbols place their ports beneath a Symbol primitive container, so valid pins such as pin1 could not be found.

The fix uses the existing _getAllPortsFromChildren path that core already relies on while initializing custom-symbol ports. It does not special-case the MOSFET, supplier part, or pin numbers.

## Validation

- Both merged custom-symbol repros pass as regular tests.
- Nine internal-connectivity tests pass across chips, interconnects, jumpers, and solder jumpers.
- bunx tsc --noEmit passes.
- Existing schematic snapshots remain unchanged.

description: Adds a repro test for the DMT6007LFG_7 MOSFET component to validate internal connections of custom-symbol pins, addressing a bug in pin resolution.
body:
## What changed

- Inlines the exact generated `DMT6007LFG_7` component from the RP2040 BLDC controller directly in the repro test.
- Uses its real custom React symbol, EasyEDA footprint, supplier metadata, CAD model metadata, and `S1`/`S2`/`S3`/`G`/`D` pin labels.
- Declares source pads 1, 2, and 3 through `internallyConnectedPins`.
- Adds the expected schematic snapshot and asserts the emitted internal connection contains pins 1, 2, and 3.
- Marks the repro with `test.failing` so the suite stays green while the bug is documented.

## Why

`NormalComponent._getInternallyConnectedPins()` currently resolves through `portMap`, which only searches direct child ports. Ports from this imported custom `<symbol>` are nested below the Symbol container, so rendering throws while resolving `pin1`.

title: Mount through-hole pin headers on top of the board, not under it
description: Fixes the mounting orientation of through-hole pin headers to ensure they are rendered on top of the board instead of underneath, correcting a significant height misrepresentation that affected enclosure design.
body:
A plain `pinrow` rendered upside down: the plastic body sat at z -3.6 to -1.6, hanging beneath the board with 2mm of pin poking up through the holes — a BOTTOM-mounted header — while `invert` produced the ordinary top-mounted one. The default and the flag were the wrong way round.

Visible in the renders (the holes met the pins at the TOP of the body rather than at its base) and worse in the numbers: the part measured **0.9mm** above the board where a 2.54mm header stands about **8.5mm**. An enclosure sized from that leaves no room for the header at all — the same class of defect as a missing body, and a worse one, because a confidently wrong height reports no `component_bounds_unknown` for anything to fall back on.

`invert` now means what it says: mounted on the underside. `faceup` and the SMD and right-angle variants are unchanged.

Separate from the body work because it changes existing renders — `pinrow6`, `pinrow6-invert`, `pinrow6-faceup`, `pinrow8_rows2`, `pinRow-smd-rightangle` — and changes what `invert` means for anything that passes it. `breakoutheaders` leaves the known-bad list in `body-envelope.test.ts` as a result.

body:
Stacked on #2144.

## Root cause

Pipeline 9 can materialize fanout traces containing a `through_obstacle` primitive. That primitive records connectivity supplied by a connected component obstacle; it is not a physical via or wire that exact DRC repair may relocate.

Joint DRC repair previously required every selected preloaded trace to become one movable high-density route. It therefore rejected a selected trace containing `through_obstacle` and stopped samples such as dataset 29 samples 3 and 6.

Keeping the complete trace fixed avoids that exception but is also incorrect ownership: it unnecessarily freezes the ordinary wire and via geometry on both sides. The dataset benchmark exposed that coarse behavior as a completion regression from 50% to 20%, primarily through additional timeouts.

## Fix

Joint repair now splits a selected preloaded trace at each `through_obstacle` primitive:

- the connectivity primitive remains fixed;
- each ordinary copper section on either side becomes a separately anchored repair connection;
- DRC errors retain the identity of the section the portfolio can move;
- repaired sections are reassembled at their original route positions around the unchanged primitive.

This directly represents repair ownership. It does not catch an error, discard connectivity, synthesize a via, or add a fallback. Missing identities, positions, routes, and overlapping repaired ranges remain explicit solver invariant errors.

## PCB snapshot

The snapshot is generated from the real dataset 29 sample 3 PCB with `circuit-to-svg`.

| Repro: Pipeline 9 stops during joint repair | Fixed: ordinary sections route around preserved connectivity |
| --- | --- |
| ![failing PCB](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/e9bc32b0d51a71b63d595fe0eeb7a5c1cf261de8/tests/repro/__snapshots__/pipeline9-through-obstacle-preloaded-trace.snap.svg) | ![fixed PCB](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/285bafefdf25e34cf8a9da15738be157b096751b/tests/repro/__snapshots__/pipeline9-through-obstacle-preloaded-trace.snap.svg) |

The test also asserts that movable ranges exclude every original `through_obstacle` position and that the final routed PCB still contains the preserved primitive.

## Results

The [full 20-sample benchmark](https://github.com/tscircuit/tscircuit-autorouter/pull/2146#issuecomment-5329944670) uses the same Pipeline 10 command and 900-second sample limit as the repro benchmark:

| Dataset 29 result | Repro PR | Coarse trace-level ownership | Section-level ownership |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Completion | 50% (10/20) | 20% (4/20) | **60% (12/20)** |
| Relaxed DRC pass | 35% (7/20) | 15% (3/20) | **35% (7/20)** |
| Timeouts | 3 | 12 | **3** |

The section-level fix restores samples 2, 5, 10, 12, 16, 17, and 20 from timeout to solved, and additionally solves the sample 3 reproduction. Samples 8, 9, and 13 remain the same independent timeout cases.

Sequential local checks use one worker:

| Dataset 29 sample | Coarse trace-level result | Section-level result | Relaxed DRC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | timeout at 900s | completes in 298.8s | pass |
| 5 | timeout at 900s | completes in 312.7s | fails; separate residual DRC work |
| 6 | completes in 882.3s | completes in 260.5s | fails; separate residual DRC work |

The visual test replays the captured real sample 3 joint-repair input, asserts the section ownership invariant, and renders the exact PCB SVG deterministically in about 2.2 seconds locally. The full benchmark completes sample 3 in 555.6 seconds under 20-worker load.

## Validation

- `bun test tests/repro/pipeline9-through-obstacle-preloaded-trace.test.ts --timeout 9999999`
- `bun test tests/features/pipeline9-joint-drc-repair-metadata.test.ts tests/features/pipeline9-drc-baseline-filter.test.ts --timeout 9999999`

- `bun run build`
- `bun run format:check`
- `./benchmark.sh --pipeline 10 --dataset 29 --sample 2 --concurrency 1 --sample-timeout 900s`
- `./benchmark.sh --pipeline 10 --dataset 29 --sample 5 --concurrency 1 --sample-timeout 900s`
- `./benchmark.sh --pipeline 10 --dataset 29 --sample 6 --concurrency 1 --sample-timeout 900s`

## Summary

- automatically link reciprocal breakout points by shared `source_trace_id`

That data was difficult to maintain and could drift from the circuit that generated it. Core already emits the PCB groups, ports, source traces, board DRC, and breakout points needed to construct the winding solver input.

Rendering the full AM62L circuit inside Cosmos also made the fixture appear stuck. Core produced 2,989 records and took about 10 seconds before the debugger appeared.

## Impact

Callers now provide Circuit JSON without repeating breakout group selectors, connection filters, layers, stackup, spacing, stagger, or differential-pair inference flags. The adapter automatically uses the single reciprocal breakout-group pair and every linked trace between it. Controls not represented by Circuit JSON, such as bus optimization metadata and optional layer hints, remain isolated under `solverOverrides`. The low-level normalized-input constructor remains supported.

The AM62L examples consume a checked-in 170-element snapshot generated from the canonical core circuit. Regeneration is explicit through `bun run generate:am62l-circuit-json`, while browser and test execution avoid the expensive core render. The circuit produces 33 linked pairs, and the byte-0, byte-1, control, and full-DDR variants all solve without precomputed layer assignments.

## Performance

- AM62L example test: about 10 seconds → about 6 ms
- Cosmos Data Bus 1 fixture: ready in about 195 ms during local browser verification
- Cosmos JavaScript build: about 10.6 MB → under 1 MB total
